lessons.title: Place Value to Hundreds
lessons.description: Extend place value to understand hundreds, tens, and ones.
lessons.formula:
A three-digit number:
345 = 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 5 ones
= 300 + 40 + 5
lessons.content:
Now that you know about tens and ones, let's go bigger! In a three-digit number, we add the hundreds place to the left of the tens. Each place is worth 10 times more than the place to its right.

In the number 352, the 3 is in the hundreds place (worth 300), the 5 is in the tens place (worth 50), and the 2 is in the ones place (worth 2). So 352 = 300 + 50 + 2.

Numbers can be written in different forms: standard form (352), expanded form (300 + 50 + 2), and word form (three hundred fifty-two).
steps: Identify the hundreds digit (leftmost): 3 = 300
Identify the tens digit (middle): 5 = 50
Identify the ones digit (rightmost): 2 = 2
Write in expanded form: 352 = 300 + 50 + 2

examples.title: Place Value of 476
examples.text: 476 = 4 hundreds + 7 tens + 6 ones = 400 + 70 + 6. The 4 is worth 400, the 7 is worth 70, and the 6 is worth 6.

examples.title: Comparing 3-Digit Numbers
examples.text: Is 529 > 497? Compare hundreds first: 5 > 4, so yes! 529 is greater than 497. You don't even need to look at the tens!

lessons.tip: When comparing three-digit numbers, ALWAYS start with the hundreds place first. If the hundreds are the same, compare the tens. If those are the same too, compare the ones. The hundreds digit has the biggest impact!

quiz.q: What is the value of the 6 in 638?
quiz.explanation: The 6 is in the hundreds place, so its value is 600.

quiz.q: Write 200 + 30 + 7 in standard form.
quiz.explanation: 200 + 30 + 7 = 237. Add the hundreds, tens, and ones together.

quiz.q: Which number is greater: 312 or 321?
quiz.explanation: Both have 3 hundreds (300). Compare tens: 2 tens (20) vs 2 tens... wait, 321 has 2 tens and 1 one vs 312 has 1 ten. Actually: 312 has 1 ten, 321 has 2 tens. Since 20 > 10, 321 > 312.

quiz.q: How many hundreds are in 500?
quiz.explanation: 500 = 5 hundreds. Each hundred is 100, and 5 × 100 = 500.

lessons.title: Addition with Regrouping
lessons.description: Add two-digit numbers when the ones add up to more than 10!
lessons.formula:
When ones add to 10 or more:
  47
+ 35
----
  82
(7+5=12, write 2 carry 1)
lessons.content:
Sometimes when you add the ones column, the sum is 10 or more. You can't fit a two-digit number in the ones place! That's when you regroup (also called carrying). You trade 10 ones for 1 ten and move it to the tens column.

For example, 47 + 35: First add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write down 2 in the ones place and carry the 1 (representing 10) to the tens column. Then add tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. The answer is 82!

Regrouping works because our number system is base-10. Every time we reach 10 in a place value, we bundle it up and move to the next place.
steps: Stack numbers vertically, lining up place values
Add the ones column first: 7 + 5 = 12
Write 2 in ones place, carry 1 to tens column
Add the tens column including the carry: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8
Write 8 in tens place. Answer: 82

examples.title: Regrouping: 58 + 34
examples.text: Ones: 8 + 4 = 12. Write 2, carry 1. Tens: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9. Answer: 92!

examples.title: Regrouping: 67 + 28
examples.text: Ones: 7 + 8 = 15. Write 5, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 2 + 1 = 9. Answer: 95!

lessons.tip: Always start adding from the RIGHT (ones column) and work left. If you forget to carry, your answer will be wrong! Double-check by estimating: 58 + 34 is about 60 + 30 = 90, so 92 makes sense.

quiz.q: What is 46 + 37?
quiz.explanation: 6 + 7 = 13 (write 3, carry 1). 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Answer: 83.

quiz.q: What is 28 + 55?
quiz.explanation: 8 + 5 = 13 (write 3, carry 1). 2 + 5 + 1 = 8. Answer: 83.

quiz.q: In regrouping, 10 ones equals what?
quiz.explanation: 10 ones = 1 ten. We regroup by trading 10 ones for 1 ten.

quiz.q: What is 39 + 43?
quiz.explanation: 9 + 3 = 12 (write 2, carry 1). 3 + 4 + 1 = 8. Wait, that's 82! Actually 9+3=12, write 2 carry 1. 3+4+1=8. Answer: 82. Hmm, let me recount: 39+43. Ones: 9+3=12, carry 1. Tens: 3+4+1=8. = 82.

lessons.title: Subtraction with Borrowing
lessons.description: Subtract two-digit numbers when you need to borrow from the tens!
lessons.formula:
When the top ones < bottom ones:
  52
- 37
----
  15
(Borrow: 12 - 7 = 5, 4 - 3 = 1)
lessons.content:
Sometimes the top digit in the ones column is smaller than the bottom digit — like trying to subtract 7 from 2. You can't do that without going negative! Instead, you borrow (regroup) from the tens column.

To solve 52 − 37: Look at the ones: 2 is less than 7. Borrow 1 ten from the 5 (making it 4), giving the ones 12. Now subtract: 12 − 7 = 5 in the ones place. Then 4 − 3 = 1 in the tens place. Answer: 15!

Borrowing is the reverse of carrying in addition. You're taking a ten and breaking it into 10 ones so you have enough to subtract.
steps: Stack numbers with the bigger number on top
Look at ones: if top < bottom, borrow from tens
Cross out the top tens digit, subtract 1, add 10 to ones
Subtract the ones column now
Subtract the tens column

examples.title: Borrowing: 63 - 28
examples.text: Ones: 3 < 8, so borrow. 6 becomes 5, 3 becomes 13. 13 - 8 = 5. Tens: 5 - 2 = 3. Answer: 35!

examples.title: Borrowing: 81 - 47
examples.text: Ones: 1 < 7, borrow. 8 becomes 7, 1 becomes 11. 11 - 7 = 4. Tens: 7 - 4 = 3. Answer: 34!

lessons.tip: If you borrow, don't forget to reduce the tens digit by 1! A common mistake is borrowing in the ones column but forgetting to change the tens. Check by adding your answer to the subtracted number: 35 + 28 = 63 ✓

quiz.q: What is 52 - 37?
quiz.explanation: Borrow: 12 - 7 = 5, 4 - 3 = 1. Answer: 15.

quiz.q: What is 70 - 43?
quiz.explanation: Borrow: 10 - 3 = 7, 6 - 4 = 2. Answer: 27.

quiz.q: What is 91 - 58?
quiz.explanation: Borrow: 11 - 8 = 3, 8 - 5 = 3. Answer: 33.

quiz.q: To subtract, when do you need to borrow?
quiz.explanation: You borrow when the top digit in a column is less than the bottom digit.

lessons.title: Advanced Skip Counting
lessons.description: Skip count by 3s, 4s, and other numbers to build multiplication skills!
lessons.content:
Skip counting by different numbers helps you build multiplication skills. When you count by 3s (3, 6, 9, 12, 15...), you are actually saying the 3-times table! Each number is 3 more than the last. Counting by 4s (4, 8, 12, 16...) follows the same pattern: add 4 each time.

These skip counting patterns appear everywhere: counting groups of 3 eggs, stacks of 4 pancakes, or rows of chairs. The more skip counting patterns you memorize, the faster you will become at multiplication and division later!
lessons.tip: Use your fingers to keep track! Each finger represents one skip count. When you count by 3s, your 1st finger is 3, 2nd is 6, 3rd is 9, and so on. This connects skip counting to multiplication facts!
steps: Choose the number to skip count by
Start at that number (or at 0)
Add the skip number each time
Say each number out loud
Continue the pattern as far as you can

examples.title: Skip Counting by 3s
examples.text: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. Each number is 3 more than the one before. This is the same as 3x1, 3x2, 3x3...

examples.title: Skip Counting by 4s
examples.text: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32. Think of it as counting groups of 4. 4x1=4, 4x2=8, 4x3=12...

quiz.q: What comes after 18 when counting by 3s?
Count by 4s: 4, 8, 12, __. What is the missing number?
What is the 5th number when counting by 3s?
quiz.explanation: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. The 5th number is 15.

lessons.title: Even and Odd Numbers
lessons.description: Learn to identify even and odd numbers and their special patterns!
lessons.formula:
Even Numbers: end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
  Can be split into 2 equal groups with nothing left over

Odd Numbers: end in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
  Always have 1 left over when paired

Rule: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 = Even
       1, 3, 5, 7, 9 = Odd
lessons.content:
Even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups with nothing left over. They always end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. For example, 8 cookies can be split into 2 groups of 4, with nothing remaining. Odd numbers always have 1 left over when you try to pair them up. They end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9.

There is a beautiful pattern on the number line: even, odd, even, odd, even, odd... all the way up! Adding two even numbers always gives an even number. Adding two odd numbers always gives an even number (the two remainders pair up). Adding one even and one odd always gives an odd number!
lessons.tip: Just look at the last digit! You do not need to check the whole number. Even numbers ALWAYS end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Odd numbers ALWAYS end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9.
steps: Look at the last digit (ones place) of the number
If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8: it is EVEN
If it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9: it is ODD
Try pairing: can you split it into 2 equal groups?
If 1 is left over, the number is odd

examples.title: Is 17 Even or Odd?
examples.text: 17 ends in 7, which is in the odd list (1, 3, 5, 7, 9). So 17 is odd. If you have 17 items, you can make 8 pairs with 1 left over.

examples.title: Is 24 Even or Odd?
examples.text: 24 ends in 4, which is in the even list (0, 2, 4, 6, 8). So 24 is even. You can split 24 into 2 groups of 12.

quiz.q: Is 23 even or odd?
quiz.explanation: 23 ends in 3, and 3 is an odd digit. So 23 is odd.

quiz.q: What is the next even number after 14?
quiz.explanation: After 14 (even) comes 15 (odd), then 16 (even). The next even number is 16.

quiz.q: If you add two odd numbers, what do you get?
quiz.explanation: Two odd numbers always add up to an even number. Example: 3 + 5 = 8.

lessons.title: Comparing 3-Digit Numbers
lessons.description: Compare numbers in the hundreds using place value!
lessons.formula:
Comparing 3-Digit Numbers:
Step 1: Compare hundreds place first
Step 2: If equal, compare tens place
Step 3: If equal, compare ones place

452 > 387 (4 > 3 in hundreds)
621 < 639 (2 < 3 in tens, hundreds equal)
547 = 547 (all places equal)
lessons.content:
Comparing 3-digit numbers uses place value. A 3-digit number has a hundreds place, a tens place, and an ones place. Always start by comparing the hundreds digit, which is the most important. If the hundreds are the same, move to the tens. If the tens are the same, compare the ones.

For example, 452 vs 387: compare hundreds first. Since 4 > 3, we know 452 > 387 without looking at the other digits! But for 621 vs 639: the hundreds are both 6, so we compare tens. Since 2 < 3, we know 621 < 639.
lessons.tip: The hundreds place is the most powerful digit in a 3-digit number. It is worth 100, while the tens is worth 10 and the ones is worth 1. Always start your comparison there!
steps: Look at the hundreds digit of both numbers
If different: the bigger hundreds digit wins
If same: look at the tens digit
If still same: look at the ones digit
Use >, <, or = to show your answer

examples.title: 452 vs 387
examples.text: Hundreds: 4 vs 3. Since 4 > 3, we know 452 > 387. The hundreds place decided it!

examples.title: 621 vs 639
examples.text: Hundreds: 6 = 6 (tie). Tens: 2 vs 3. Since 2 < 3, we get 621 < 639. Had to go to the tens place!

quiz.q: Which is bigger: 523 or 498?
quiz.explanation: Hundreds: 5 > 4, so 523 > 498.

quiz.q: Compare: 371 ___ 371
quiz.explanation: Both numbers are exactly the same, so 371 = 371.

quiz.q: Which is smaller: 256 or 265?
quiz.explanation: Hundreds equal (2=2). Tens: 5 < 6, so 256 < 265.

lessons.title: Introduction to US Coins
lessons.description: Identify pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters and learn their values. Count combinations of coins!
lessons.formula:
US Coin Values:

Penny  = 1¢
Nickel  = 5¢
Dime    = 10¢
Quarter = 25¢

Counting Coins:
Add the values of all coins together
Example: 2 quarters + 1 dime + 3 pennies
= 50¢ + 10¢ + 3¢ = 63¢
lessons.content:
The United States uses four main coins in everyday life: the penny (1¢), nickel (5¢), dime (10¢), and quarter (25¢). Each coin has a different size, color, and picture on the front (the "heads" side), making them easy to tell apart once you learn their features.

The penny is copper-colored and shows President Abraham Lincoln. It is worth just 1 cent — the smallest value. The nickel is silver-colored, larger than a penny, and shows Thomas Jefferson. It is worth 5 cents, which is the same as five pennies. The dime is the smallest coin by size but is worth 10 cents — more than the nickel! It shows Franklin D. Roosevelt. The quarter is the largest of the four coins and shows George Washington. It is worth 25 cents.

When you have a collection of coins, you count the total value by adding each coin's value. Grouping same coins together first makes counting easier. For example, if you have 3 dimes and 2 nickels, count: 3 × 10¢ + 2 × 5¢ = 30¢ + 10¢ = 40¢.
steps: Learn each coin's name, appearance, and value by heart
Sort coins into groups: all pennies together, all nickels together, etc.
Skip-count each group: pennies by 1s, nickels by 5s, dimes by 10s, quarters by 25s
Add the total from each group to find the grand total
Write the total using the ¢ symbol (e.g., 47¢) or in dollars (e.g., $0.47)

examples.title: Counting Mixed Coins
examples.text:
You have 1 quarter, 2 dimes, 1 nickel, and 3 pennies.

Quarters: 1 × 25¢ = 25¢
Dimes: 2 × 10¢ = 20¢
Nickel: 1 × 5¢ = 5¢
Pennies: 3 × 1¢ = 3¢

Total: 25¢ + 20¢ + 5¢ + 3¢ = 53¢

examples.title: How Many Pennies Equal a Quarter?
examples.text:
A quarter = 25¢. A penny = 1¢.

25¢ ÷ 1¢ = 25 pennies

So it takes 25 pennies to equal one quarter!

lessons.tip: Practice with real coins at home! Ask a family member to give you a handful of coins and try to count the total. Start by sorting them into groups, then skip-count each group before adding everything together. You'll become a coin-counting expert in no time!

quiz.q: Which coin is worth 10 cents?
quiz.explanation: A dime is worth 10¢. Penny=1¢, Nickel=5¢, Quarter=25¢.

quiz.q: You have 2 quarters and 1 dime. How much money do you have?
quiz.explanation: 2 quarters = 50¢, 1 dime = 10¢. Wait — 50 + 10 = 60¢! The answer is 60¢.

quiz.q: How many nickels make 25 cents?
quiz.explanation: Each nickel = 5¢. 25¢ ÷ 5¢ = 5 nickels. Five nickels equal one quarter.

lessons.title: Mental Math: Making Tens and Doubles
lessons.description: Use smart mental math strategies to add and subtract quickly without paper!
lessons.formula:
Mental Math Strategies:
Doubles: 6+6=12, 7+7=14, 8+8=16
Near Doubles: 6+7=13 (6+6+1)
Make Ten: 8+5=8+2+3=10+3=13
Break Apart: 47+23 = 40+20+7+3 = 60+10 = 70
lessons.content:
Mental math means solving problems in your head without writing anything down! Good mental math starts with knowing a few key strategies. The doubles strategy uses facts you've memorized: 6+6=12, 7+7=14, 8+8=16. If you know your doubles, you can solve near-doubles too: 6+7 is just one more than 6+6, so it equals 13!

The make-ten strategy is incredibly powerful. For 8+5, break the 5 into 2+3. Now 8+2=10, and 10+3=13. By making a friendly ten first, the rest of the problem becomes easy! This works for bigger numbers too: 38+7, break 7 into 2+5, so 38+2=40, then 40+5=45.

The break apart strategy lets you add the tens and ones separately. For 47+23, add the tens (40+20=60) and the ones (7+3=10), then combine (60+10=70). These three strategies — doubles, make-ten, and break apart — will let you solve most addition problems mentally!
steps: Look at the numbers: are they doubles or near-doubles?
Can you make a ten? Break one number to complete a ten
Can you break apart by place value? Add tens first, then ones
Use the strategy that feels fastest for that particular problem
Always check: does your answer make sense?

examples.title: Near Doubles
examples.text: 7+8: Since 7+7=14, then 7+8 is just one more: 15! You used the near-doubles strategy.

examples.title: Make Ten
examples.text: 9+6: Break 6 into 1+5. Now 9+1=10, then 10+5=15. Making ten first made this easy!

lessons.tip: Play mental math games! Have someone say two numbers and race to add them first. Start with smaller numbers and work up. The faster you get, the more confidence you'll build!

quiz.q: Use near doubles: 8 + 9 = ?
quiz.explanation: 8+8=16, so 8+9 is one more: 17!

quiz.q: Use make-ten: 7 + 5 = ?
Break apart 34 + 22:
Which strategy is best for 6 + 6?
quiz.explanation: 6+6 is a perfect doubles fact! No strategy needed — you just know it!

lessons.title: Estimation and Rounding to the Nearest Ten
lessons.description: Round numbers to the nearest ten and estimate answers to check if they make sense!
lessons.formula:
Rounding to the Nearest Ten:
Find the midpoint (the 5):
- Numbers 0-4 round DOWN
- Numbers 5-9 round UP

23 -> rounds to 20 (closer to 20)
27 -> rounds to 30 (closer to 30)
25 -> rounds to 30 (5 or above rounds up!)
lessons.content:
Rounding means replacing a number with a nearby number that's easier to work with. When you round to the nearest ten, 23 becomes 20 and 27 becomes 30. This is useful for estimating — quickly figuring out about how much something is without calculating exactly.

Here's the rounding rule: look at the ones digit. If it's 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, round DOWN to the lower ten. If it's 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, round UP to the higher ten. Think of 5 as the tipping point — five or more means you 'round up.' So 34 rounds to 30, but 35 rounds to 40!

Why does this matter? Imagine you're at the store and buy items costing $13, $28, and $9. You can round each to the nearest ten: $10, $30, and $10. That's about $50 total. This estimate tells you roughly what to expect. If the cashier says $150, you know something is wrong! Estimating is a real-world superpower.
steps: Look at the number you want to round (e.g., 46)
Find the ones digit: 6
Is the ones digit 5 or more? Yes — so round UP
Change the ones digit to 0 and add 1 to the tens: 46 -> 50
If ones digit was 4 or less, keep the tens and make ones 0: 43 -> 40

examples.title: Rounding to Nearest Ten
examples.text: Round 62: ones digit is 2 (less than 5), round DOWN to 60. Round 67: ones digit is 7 (5 or more), round UP to 70. Round 65: ones digit is exactly 5, round UP to 70!

examples.title: Estimating a Sum
examples.text: Estimate 28 + 43 + 15: Round each to the nearest ten: 30 + 40 + 10 = 80. The exact answer is 86, and our estimate of 80 is close — it's reasonable!

lessons.tip: The 'five or higher, round up' rule is easy to remember! Draw a number line and mark 35 in the middle. 31, 32, 33, 34 are closer to 30 (round down). 36, 37, 38, 39 are closer to 40 (round up). And 35? The tiebreaker goes UP!

quiz.q: What does 47 round to (nearest ten)?
quiz.explanation: Ones digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so round UP to 50.

quiz.q: What does 32 round to (nearest ten)?
quiz.explanation: Ones digit is 2, which is less than 5, so round DOWN to 30.

quiz.q: Estimate: 19 + 22 + 31 (round each first)
quiz.explanation: Round: 20 + 20 + 30 = 70. The exact answer is 72, very close!

quiz.q: What is the rule for the ones digit 5?
quiz.explanation: When the ones digit is 5 or higher, we always round UP to the next ten.

lessons.title: Standard Measurement: Inches and Centimeters
lessons.description: Measure objects using rulers in both inches and centimeters!
lessons.formula:
Measurement Units:
Customary: 12 inches = 1 foot
Metric: 100 centimeters = 1 meter

Always start measuring from the ZERO mark!
Line up the edge of the object with 0.
lessons.content:
Measuring length means finding out how long something is using a tool like a ruler. There are two main measurement systems. The customary system (used in the US) measures in inches, feet, and yards. The metric system (used around the world) measures in centimeters and meters.

When using a ruler, the most important rule is: always start at zero! Line up one end of your object exactly with the 0 mark on the ruler. Then look at where the other end reaches. If it reaches the mark labeled 5, your object is 5 inches (or 5 centimeters, depending on your ruler).

An inch is about the width of your thumb, while a centimeter is about the width of your pinky finger. Inches are bigger than centimeters — in fact, 1 inch is about 2.5 centimeters! Both systems work perfectly for measuring; they just use different sized units. Scientists and most of the world use metric, while the US uses customary for everyday measurements.
steps: Choose your ruler (inches or centimeters)
Place the object on the ruler with one end at the ZERO mark
Look straight down at the other end of the object
Read the number where the object ends
Include units: 'The pencil is 6 inches long' or '15 centimeters'

examples.title: Measuring a Pencil
examples.text: Place a pencil on an inch ruler starting at 0. The tip reaches the 7 mark. The pencil is 7 inches long! On a centimeter ruler, the same pencil might reach about 18 centimeters.

examples.title: Comparing Measurements
examples.text: A book is 10 inches long. A tablet is 8 inches long. The book is longer by 2 inches! You can compare any two measurements by subtracting.

lessons.tip: Practice measuring everything! Your desk, your shoe, a leaf, your lunchbox. Estimate first, then measure to see how close you were. This builds both estimation and measurement skills!

quiz.q: You line up a crayon at 0 and the tip reaches 4 on an inch ruler. How long is the crayon?
quiz.explanation: Always read the number at the end of the object. Since the crayon ends at 4, it's 4 inches.

quiz.q: Which is longer: something that is 3 inches or 3 centimeters?
quiz.explanation: An inch is much bigger than a centimeter (about 2.5x bigger). So 3 inches > 3 cm.

quiz.q: What is the most important rule when measuring?
quiz.explanation: Always line up the object with the zero mark! If you start at the wrong place, your measurement will be wrong.

quiz.q: About how many centimeters equal 1 inch?
quiz.explanation: 1 inch is about 2.5 centimeters. That's why centimeter numbers are always bigger for the same object.

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000
lessons.description: Add and subtract three-digit numbers using place value strategies and regrouping!
lessons.formula:
Three-Digit Addition:
  357
+ 284
-----
  641

Add ones: 7+4=11 (write 1, carry 1)
Add tens: 5+8+1=14 (write 4, carry 1)
Add hundreds: 3+2+1=6
lessons.content:
Adding and subtracting numbers up to 1,000 uses the same strategies as two-digit numbers, but now you work with hundreds, tens, and ones columns. The key is to always start from the ones place and work left, regrouping when any column adds to 10 or more.

For example, to add 357 + 284: start with ones — 7 + 4 = 11. Write 1 and carry the 1 to the tens column. Then tens — 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4 and carry 1 to hundreds. Then hundreds — 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The answer is 641! Each column works the same way as before, you just have an extra column for hundreds.

You can also use the expanded form strategy: 357 + 284 = (300 + 50 + 7) + (200 + 80 + 4) = (300+200) + (50+80) + (7+4) = 500 + 130 + 11 = 641. This breaks the problem into easier parts. Both methods give the same answer — use whichever feels more natural!
steps: Line up the numbers by place value (hundreds over hundreds, etc.)
Start adding in the ONES column
If the sum is 10 or more: write the ones digit, carry the tens digit
Move to the TENS column and add (including any carried digit)
Move to the HUNDREDS column and add (including any carried digit)
Read your answer and check if it's reasonable

examples.title: Three-Digit Addition with Regrouping
examples.text: Add 468 + 275: Ones: 8+5=13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 6+7+1=14, write 4 carry 1. Hundreds: 4+2+1=7. Answer: 743!

examples.title: Three-Digit Subtraction
examples.text: Subtract 523 - 187: Ones: 3-7 can't do, borrow from tens: 13-7=6. Tens: 1-8 can't do, borrow from hundreds: 11-8=3. Hundreds: 4-1=3. Answer: 336!

lessons.tip: When regrouping, cross out the digit you borrowed from and write the new number above it. This keeps your work neat and helps you avoid mistakes. Always double-check by adding your answer back!

quiz.q: When adding 3 digits in the ones column and getting 16, what do you do?
quiz.explanation: Write the ones digit (6) in the ones column and carry the tens digit (1) to the tens column.

quiz.q: Estimate: 312 + 489 (round to nearest hundred)
quiz.explanation: Round: 300 + 500 = 800. The exact answer is 801, very close!

lessons.title: Partitioning Rectangles into Rows and Columns
lessons.description: Divide rectangles into equal rows and columns to build early multiplication understanding!
lessons.formula:
Rectangle Partitioning:
3 rows x 4 columns = 12 squares total
Total = rows x columns
Total = columns x rows
(Commutative property!)
lessons.content:
When you divide a rectangle into equal rows (going across) and columns (going up and down), you create a grid called an array. Arrays are a visual way to understand multiplication! If your rectangle has 3 rows and 4 columns, you can count all the squares: there are 12 in total. That's because 3 x 4 = 12.

Rows go left to right, like seats in a movie theater. Columns go up and down, like pillars in a building. When you partition a rectangle into 3 rows and 4 columns, every row has exactly 4 squares, and every column has exactly 3 squares. This arrangement of equal groups is the foundation of multiplication!

You can write the total as either 3 x 4 or 4 x 3 — the answer is the same either way (this is the commutative property). Think of it as '3 rows of 4' or '4 columns of 3' — both give you 12 squares. Drawing and counting arrays builds the visual understanding that makes multiplication click!
steps: Draw a rectangle on grid paper
Decide how many rows (horizontal) you want
Draw lines to create equal rows
Decide how many columns (vertical) you want
Draw lines to create equal columns
Count the total squares: multiply rows x columns

examples.title: Rows and Columns
examples.text: A rectangle has 4 rows and 5 columns. Count: Row 1 has 5, Row 2 has 5, Row 3 has 5, Row 4 has 5. Total: 4 x 5 = 20 squares!

examples.title: Real-World Arrays
examples.text: A chocolate bar has 6 rows with 3 pieces in each row. That's a 6 x 3 array = 18 pieces total. The packaging IS a rectangle partition!

lessons.tip: Use dot stickers on graph paper to create arrays! Make different arrays that equal the same total (like 12 = 3x4 = 2x6 = 1x12). See how many different rectangle arrays you can find for each number!

quiz.q: A rectangle has 5 rows and 3 columns. How many squares total?
quiz.explanation: 5 x 3 = 15. Five rows of three equals fifteen squares.

quiz.q: Which arrays make 24 squares?
quiz.explanation: 24 = 1x24, 2x12, 3x8, 4x6. All of these are valid arrays!

quiz.q: If an array has 7 columns and 2 rows, how many total?
quiz.explanation: 7 x 2 = 14. Seven columns times two rows equals fourteen.

quiz.q: Rows go which direction?
quiz.explanation: Rows go left to right (horizontal). Columns go up and down (vertical).

lessons.title: Compare and Combine Word Problems
lessons.description: Solve comparison (how many more) and combination (total) word problems!
lessons.formula:
Word Problem Types:
Combine (total): Tom has 5. Sara has 7. Total = 5 + 7 = 12
Compare (difference): Tom has 5. Sara has 7. Who has more? 7 - 5 = 2 more
Key words: 'more', 'fewer', 'altogether', 'in all'
lessons.content:
Word problems come in different types, and knowing the type helps you choose the right operation. Combine problems ask you to put groups together to find a total — use addition. Key words include 'altogether,' 'in all,' 'combined,' and 'total.' Compare problems ask you to find the difference between two amounts — use subtraction. Key words include 'how many more,' 'how many fewer,' and 'what is the difference.'

For example: 'Tom has 15 stickers. Sara has 9. How many more stickers does Tom have?' This is a compare problem — subtract: 15 - 9 = 6. Tom has 6 more stickers. If the question were 'How many stickers do they have altogether?' that would be a combine problem — add: 15 + 9 = 24.

A powerful tool for word problems is the bar model (also called a tape diagram). Draw two bars of different lengths to represent the two quantities. The difference bar shows the comparison, and combining both bars shows the total. Visual models make word problems much easier to solve!
steps: Read the problem carefully — what is it asking?
Identify the numbers and what they represent
Look for key words: 'more/fewer' = compare (subtract), 'altogether/total' = combine (add)
Draw a bar model to visualize the situation
Write the equation and solve
Check: does your answer make sense in the story?

examples.title: Compare Problem
examples.text: A red ribbon is 18 cm. A blue ribbon is 12 cm. How much longer is the red ribbon? Compare: 18 - 12 = 6 cm. The red ribbon is 6 cm longer.

examples.title: Combine Problem
examples.text: Maya read 23 pages on Monday and 17 pages on Tuesday. How many pages did she read in all? Combine: 23 + 17 = 40 pages total!

lessons.tip: Always RE-READ the question after solving to make sure you answered what was actually asked! The most common mistake is solving the wrong type of problem.

quiz.q: 'Sam has 12 apples. Lee has 8. How many MORE apples does Sam have?' What type?
quiz.explanation: 'How many MORE' is a compare problem. Subtract: 12 - 8 = 4 more apples.

quiz.q: 'There are 7 birds on a fence and 5 in a tree. How many birds IN ALL?' What type?
quiz.explanation: 'In all' means combine. Add: 7 + 5 = 12 birds total.

quiz.q: Solve: Mia has 22 stickers. Jake has 15. How many fewer does Jake have?
quiz.explanation: Compare: 22 - 15 = 7. Jake has 7 fewer stickers.

quiz.q: The zoo has 14 lions and 9 tigers. How many animals total?
quiz.explanation: Combine: 14 + 9 = 23 animals total at the zoo.

lessons.title: Introduction to Multiplication
lessons.description: Understand multiplication as repeated addition using arrays!
lessons.formula:
Multiplication = Repeated Addition
3 × 4 = 3 groups of 4
= 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
An array shows rows × columns
lessons.content:
Multiplication is a fast way of adding the same number over and over! Instead of 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, we write 3 × 4 = 12. The × symbol means 'groups of' or 'times.' The answer is called the product.

An array is a picture of multiplication using rows and columns. 3 rows of 4 objects makes a 3 × 4 array with 12 total objects. Arrays help you SEE multiplication!

You use multiplication more than you think! If you have 3 bags with 4 apples each, that's 3 × 4 = 12 apples total. Much faster than counting 4 + 4 + 4!
steps: Identify the number of groups (first factor)
Identify how many in each group (second factor)
Write as repeated addition: 3 × 4 = 4 + 4 + 4
Add them up: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Draw an array to visualize: 3 rows of 4

examples.title: Arrays: 3 × 4
examples.text: Draw 3 rows with 4 dots in each row: •••• / •••• / ••••. Count them all: 12 dots! 3 × 4 = 12.

examples.title: Word Problem: Cookies
examples.text: You bake 5 trays of cookies with 3 cookies on each tray. That's 5 groups of 3. 5 × 3 = 15 cookies total!

lessons.tip: Start by memorizing the ×2, ×5, and ×10 facts — they're the easiest because they connect to skip counting! ×2 is counting by 2s, ×5 is counting by 5s, and ×10 is counting by 10s.

quiz.q: What is 3 × 4?
What is 5 × 3?
Which repeated addition equals 4 × 2?
quiz.explanation: 4 × 2 means 4 groups of 2, or 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.

quiz.q: If you have 6 bags with 2 candies each, how many candies total?
quiz.explanation: 6 bags × 2 candies = 6 × 2 = 12 candies.

lessons.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition
lessons.description: Build multiplication understanding by adding equal groups together!
lessons.formula:
Multiplication = Repeated Addition
3 groups of 4 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
So: 3 x 4 = 12

Groups x Items per group = Total
5 x 2 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10
lessons.content:
Multiplication is a fast way of adding equal groups. Instead of writing 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4, you can write 5 x 4 = 20. The first number tells you how many groups, and the second tells you how many items are in each group. The answer is called the product.

Think about real life: if you have 3 bags with 4 apples in each bag, you could count 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, or simply multiply 3 x 4 = 12. Multiplication is the shortcut that makes math faster! Understanding it as repeated addition helps you see why it works.
lessons.tip: Draw circles to represent groups and dots inside for items! For 3 x 4, draw 3 circles with 4 dots each. Count all the dots to get 12. This visual approach makes multiplication concrete.
steps: Identify the number of groups (first number)
Identify how many items in each group (second number)
Write as repeated addition: add the second number as many times as the first
Count the total
Write the multiplication equation: groups x items = total

examples.title: 4 Groups of 3
examples.text: 4 groups of 3 cookies = 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 cookies. As multiplication: 4 x 3 = 12.

examples.title: 2 Groups of 7
examples.text: 2 shelves with 7 books each = 7 + 7 = 14 books. As multiplication: 2 x 7 = 14.

quiz.q: What is 3 x 5 as repeated addition?
quiz.explanation: 3 x 5 means 3 groups of 5, so 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

quiz.q: 4 groups of 2 equals what?
Which shows 5 x 3 as repeated addition?
quiz.explanation: 5 x 3 = 5 groups of 3 = 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3... wait, no! 5 groups of 3 means 3 repeated 5 times = 3+3+3+3+3. But 5 x 3 = 3+3+3+3+3, which is answer C. Actually, the answer is C: 3+3+3+3+3 = 15.

lessons.title: Arrays and Equal Groups
lessons.description: Use arrays (rows and columns) to model multiplication!
lessons.formula:
Array = Rectangular Arrangement
Rows x Columns = Total

Example: 3 rows, 4 columns
x x x x
x x x x
x x x x
3 x 4 = 12 dots total
lessons.content:
An array is a rectangular arrangement of objects in rows and columns. Every row has the same number of objects, and every column has the same number. Arrays are a powerful visual tool for understanding multiplication because they show equal groups in an organized way.

If you have 3 rows with 4 objects in each row, that is the multiplication fact 3 x 4 = 12. You can count by rows (4 + 4 + 4 = 12) or by columns (3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12). Both give the same answer! Arrays also show that multiplication is commutative: 3 x 4 = 4 x 3 = 12.
lessons.tip: Arrays are everywhere: egg cartons (2 x 6), ice cube trays (2 x 8 or 4 x 4), bookshelves, windows. Start noticing arrays in the real world and practice multiplying rows x columns!
steps: Identify the number of rows (across)
Identify the number of columns (down)
Each row is one group of items
Multiply: rows x columns = total
Check by counting all items or flipping: columns x rows

examples.title: Cookie Array
examples.text: A baking sheet has 4 rows of 5 cookies. 4 x 5 = 20 cookies. You can also count by columns: 5 rows of 4 = 20. Same answer!

examples.title: Chairs in a Classroom
examples.text: 6 rows of 3 desks = 18 desks total. 6 x 3 = 18. You could also say 3 columns of 6 = 18. Arrays show multiplication goes both ways!

quiz.q: An array has 3 rows and 5 columns. How many items total?
quiz.explanation: 3 x 5 = 15 items.

quiz.q: Which multiplication fact matches 4 rows of 2?
quiz.explanation: 4 rows of 2 = 4 x 2 = 8.

quiz.q: 2 x 6 and 6 x 2 give the same result. This is called:
quiz.explanation: The commutative property says you can flip the numbers in multiplication and get the same answer.

lessons.title: Fractions: Halves, Thirds, Fourths
lessons.description: Identify and compare basic fractions of shapes and sets!
lessons.formula:
A fraction has a numerator (top) and denominator (bottom):
½ = 1 of 2 equal parts
⅓ = 1 of 3 equal parts
¼ = 1 of 4 equal parts
lessons.content:
A fraction describes equal parts of a whole. The top number is the numerator (how many parts you have) and the bottom is the denominator (how many equal parts total). A unit fraction always has 1 as the numerator (½, ⅓, ¼).

When you divide a shape into halves, it's split into 2 equal parts. Thirds = 3 equal parts. Fourths (or quarters) = 4 equal parts. The parts MUST be equal for it to be a fair fraction!

You can also show fractions of a group. If you have 6 markers and 3 are red, then 3/6 of the markers are red. That simplifies to ½!
steps: Count the total number of EQUAL parts (denominator)
Count how many parts you're interested in (numerator)
Write as numerator/denominator
Verify all parts are equal in size
For shapes, make sure lines divide evenly

examples.title: Shading Fractions
examples.text: A pizza cut into 4 equal slices. You shade 1 slice. That's ¼ (one fourth) of the pizza shaded.

examples.title: Fractions of a Set
examples.text: A box has 8 crayons: 3 red, 2 blue, 3 green. The fraction of red crayons is 3/8.

lessons.tip: The denominator (bottom) is always the TOTAL number of equal parts, and the numerator (top) is the number of parts you're focusing on. Think: 'numerator sounds like newer — it's the number on top that's new to you!'

quiz.q: In the fraction ¾, what does the 4 represent?
quiz.explanation: The denominator (4) is the total number of equal parts the whole is divided into.

quiz.q: If a rectangle is divided into 3 equal parts and you color 2, what fraction is colored?
quiz.explanation: 2 parts out of 3 equal parts = 2/3.

quiz.q: Which is larger: ½ or ¼?
quiz.explanation: When you split something into only 2 parts (halves), each piece is bigger than when you split into 4 parts (fourths). So ½ > ¼.

quiz.q: What is a unit fraction?
quiz.explanation: A unit fraction has a numerator of 1, like ½, ⅓, ¼, etc.

lessons.title: Measurement & Geometry Basics
lessons.description: Measure objects and explore more geometric shapes!
lessons.formula:
Units of Length:
1 meter (m) = 100 centimeters (cm)
Tools: ruler, meter stick, measuring tape
lessons.content:
Measuring accurately is an important real-world skill. In second grade, you'll use centimeters (cm) and meters (m) to describe how long things are. A ruler shows centimeters, and a meter stick shows meters.

1 meter = 100 centimeters. A meter is about the width of a doorway! You'd use centimeters for smaller things like a pencil, and meters for bigger things like a room.

In geometry, a polygon is any closed shape with straight sides. A quadrilateral is a polygon with exactly 4 sides — squares, rectangles, rhombuses, and trapezoids are all quadrilaterals!
steps: Choose the right tool: ruler for small things, meter stick for large
Line up the zero mark of the ruler with one end of the object
Read the number at the other end of the object
Estimate first, then measure to check your estimate
Count sides and angles to classify polygons

examples.title: Measuring a Book
examples.text: A book is about 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. Use a ruler and line up the 0 mark with the edge of the book.

examples.title: Quadrilaterals
examples.text: A square has 4 equal sides. A rectangle has 4 sides with opposite sides equal. Both are quadrilaterals! A trapezoid is also a quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides.

lessons.tip: Always estimate BEFORE you measure! It trains your eye and helps you catch mistakes. If you estimate a pencil is about 15 cm but measure it as 150 cm, you'll know something went wrong!

quiz.q: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?
quiz.explanation: 1 meter = 100 centimeters. 'Centi' means hundred!

quiz.q: Which tool is best for measuring a pencil?
quiz.explanation: A ruler is perfect for measuring small objects like a pencil (usually 15-20 cm).

quiz.q: How many sides does a quadrilateral have?
quiz.explanation: 'Quad' means four! A quadrilateral has 4 sides. Examples: square, rectangle, trapezoid.

quiz.q: Which would you measure in meters?
quiz.explanation: A classroom is large, so meters are the appropriate unit. Small objects use centimeters.

lessons.title: Time to 5 Minutes
lessons.description: Read analog and digital clocks to the nearest 5 minutes!
lessons.formula:
Minutes on a Clock:
Each number = 5 minutes
1 = 5 min, 2 = 10 min, 3 = 15 min
4 = 20 min, 5 = 25 min, 6 = 30 min
7 = 35 min, 8 = 40 min, 9 = 45 min
10 = 50 min, 11 = 55 min, 12 = 60 min (0)

Shortcut: Count by 5s!
lessons.content:
On an analog clock, each number represents 5 minutes. When the minute hand points to the 1, it means 5 minutes past the hour. When it points to the 3, it means 15 minutes past (also called quarter past). When it points to the 6, it means 30 minutes past (half past). When it points to the 9, it means 45 minutes past (quarter to the next hour).

To read the time, first check the hour hand to find the hour, then check where the minute hand points. If the minute hand is between numbers, count by 5s from the 12. For example, if the minute hand is on the 4, the time is 20 minutes past the hour. If it is one tick past the 4, it is 21 minutes past.
lessons.tip: Skip count by 5s to quickly tell the minutes! Point at each number on the clock and count: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. Memorizing these helps you read any clock instantly!
steps: Find the hour hand (short): which number is it past?
Find the minute hand (long): which number does it point to?
Multiply the minute number by 5 to get the minutes
If between numbers, count the small ticks past the last number
Say the time: hour:minutes

examples.title: Reading 3:25
examples.text: Hour hand is past 3, minute hand points to 5. 5 x 5 = 25 minutes. The time is 3:25, or 'twenty-five past three.'

examples.title: Reading 7:40
examples.text: Hour hand is past 7, minute hand points to 8. 8 x 5 = 40 minutes. The time is 7:40, or 'twenty to eight.'

quiz.q: If the minute hand points to the 4, how many minutes past the hour is it?
quiz.explanation: 4 x 5 = 20 minutes past the hour.

quiz.q: What is another way to say 15 minutes past the hour?
quiz.explanation: 15 minutes = a quarter of an hour, so 15 minutes past is 'quarter past.'

quiz.q: The minute hand points to the 9. How many minutes is that?
quiz.explanation: 9 x 5 = 45 minutes.

lessons.title: Money Word Problems
lessons.description: Solve real-world problems involving adding and subtracting money!
lessons.formula:
Money Strategies:
Adding: line up decimal points
Subtracting: line up decimal points

Counting up for change:
Purchase: $0.47
Paid: $1.00
Count up: 47 to 50 = 3 cents
         50 to 100 = 50 cents
Change: 3 + 50 = 53 cents
lessons.content:
Money word problems ask you to add, subtract, or compare amounts of money. The key is to read carefully, identify what the question is asking, and choose the right operation. Always remember to write dollar amounts with a decimal point and two digits for cents: $1.50, not $1.5.

When finding change, you can subtract (amount paid minus cost) or count up from the cost to the amount paid. Counting up is often easier! For example, if something costs $0.47 and you pay with $1.00: count from 47 to 50 (3 cents), then from 50 to 100 (50 cents). Change = 53 cents.
lessons.tip: When adding money, always line up the decimal points! Just like with regular addition, start from the right (cents) and work left. And remember: 100 cents = 1 dollar.
steps: Read the problem carefully, underline the question
Identify what you know (prices, amounts)
Decide: add to find total, subtract to find change or difference
Write the equation with dollar signs and decimals
Solve and write the answer with a dollar sign

examples.title: Buying Treats
examples.text: A pencil costs 35 cents and an eraser costs 28 cents. How much for both? 35 + 28 = 63 cents. Total cost is $0.63.

examples.title: Making Change
examples.text: You buy a book for $1.25 and pay with $2.00. Count up: 1.25 to 1.50 = 25 cents, 1.50 to 2.00 = 50 cents. Change = 75 cents ($0.75).

quiz.q: A toy costs $0.85 and a candy costs $0.45. How much do they cost together?
You pay $1.00 for a 67-cent sticker. What is your change?
quiz.explanation: Count up: 67 to 70 = 3 cents, 70 to 100 = 30 cents. 3 + 30 = 33 cents.

quiz.q: Which costs more: a 52-cent eraser or a 48-cent pencil?
quiz.explanation: 52 cents > 48 cents, so the eraser costs more.

lessons.title: Fraction Models
lessons.description: Use shapes and number lines to model and understand fractions!
lessons.formula:
Fraction = Parts / Total
Numerator (top) = parts shaded or counted
Denominator (bottom) = total equal parts

1/3 = 1 out of 3 equal parts
2/3 = 2 out of 3 equal parts

Number line: 0 to 1 divided into equal sections
lessons.content:
Fraction models help you see what fractions look like. You can use shapes divided into equal parts, or you can use a number line from 0 to 1. When shading shapes, the number of shaded parts is the numerator (top) and the total number of equal parts is the denominator (bottom).

On a number line, the space between 0 and 1 is divided into equal sections. If divided into 3 equal parts, each part is 1/3. The first mark after 0 is 1/3, the second is 2/3, and 3/3 = 1 (the whole). Fraction models make abstract fractions concrete and easy to understand!
lessons.tip: Equal parts are absolutely essential! If a shape is divided into uneven pieces, you CANNOT make a proper fraction from it. Always double-check that all parts are the same size.
steps: Divide the shape into equal parts (or divide the number line 0 to 1)
Count the total number of equal parts = denominator
Count the shaded or selected parts = numerator
Write the fraction: numerator/numerator
Check: are all parts truly equal?

examples.title: Modeling 2/3
examples.text: Divide a rectangle into 3 equal parts. Shade 2 of them. The fraction is 2/3. On a number line from 0 to 1 divided into thirds, 2/3 is the second mark.

examples.title: Modeling 3/4 on a Number Line
examples.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Divide it into 4 equal sections. 3/4 is the third mark from 0. Each section represents 1/4.

quiz.q: A circle is divided into 6 equal parts and 2 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
quiz.explanation: 2 parts shaded out of 6 total equal parts = 2/6.

quiz.q: On a number line from 0 to 1 divided into 4 parts, what is the third mark?
quiz.explanation: Each section is 1/4. The third mark is 3/4.

quiz.q: Which fraction model shows 1/3?
options: 1 shaded part out of 3 equal parts
quiz.explanation: 1/3 means 1 part shaded out of 3 equal total parts.

lessons.title: Bar Graphs and Pictographs
lessons.description: Read and interpret bar graphs and pictographs to analyze data!
lessons.formula:
Reading Bar Graphs:
1. Read title and labels
2. Check the scale (what each bar mark represents)
3. Read each bar's height
4. Compare bars to answer questions

Scale Examples:
1 square = 1 item
1 square = 2 items
1 square = 5 items
lessons.content:
Bar graphs use bars of different heights to show data. The taller the bar, the more of that category there is. The horizontal axis (bottom) shows the categories, and the vertical axis (side) shows the amount, using a scale that tells you how much each mark is worth.

Pictographs use pictures instead of bars. Each picture represents a certain number of items (shown in the key). Both types of graphs help you quickly compare categories, find the most and least, and answer questions about data. Always check the scale or key before reading the graph!
lessons.tip: Always check the scale or key BEFORE you start reading! If the scale is 'each square = 5' but you read it as 'each square = 1,' every answer will be 5 times too small.
steps: Read the title to understand what data is shown
Check the scale (bar graph) or key (pictograph)
Read each bar or count each symbol
Find totals: add up all bars or symbols
Compare: which is most? least? how much more?

examples.title: Reading a Bar Graph
examples.text: A bar graph shows favorite colors: Red=8, Blue=12, Green=5. The scale is 1 mark = 1 vote. Blue (12) has the most votes, Green (5) has the fewest.

examples.title: Reading a Pictograph
examples.text: A pictograph shows pets: dogs have 4 symbols, cats have 3. Key: 1 symbol = 2 pets. Dogs=8, Cats=6. Dogs are more popular by 2 pets.

quiz.q: On a bar graph with scale '1 mark = 2 votes,' a bar reaches the 5th mark. How many votes?
quiz.explanation: 5 marks x 2 votes each = 10 votes.

quiz.q: What does the key on a pictograph tell you?
quiz.explanation: The key explains the value of each picture/symbol in the pictograph.

quiz.q: If Bar A reaches 4 and Bar B reaches 7 (scale 1), how much more does B have?
quiz.explanation: 7 - 4 = 3. Bar B has 3 more.

lessons.title: Line Plots
lessons.description: Create and read line plots to organize and analyze measurement data!
lessons.formula:
Line Plot:
Number line on the bottom
X marks stacked above each number
Each X = one data point

Reading:
Count X's at each value
Most X's = most common value
Tallest stack = mode (most frequent)
lessons.content:
A line plot is a simple way to show data on a number line. For each data point, you place an X above the matching number. If multiple items have the same value, you stack the X's on top of each other. This makes it easy to see which values appear most often and how the data is spread out.

Line plots are perfect for showing measurement data, like the lengths of pencils in your class or the number of books each student read. To read a line plot, count the X's above each number to find how many items have that value. The tallest stack shows the most common value!
lessons.tip: Always count every X carefully! It is easy to miscount when X's are stacked. Use your finger to point at each X as you count to avoid mistakes.
steps: Draw a number line with the possible values marked
For each data point, put an X above its value
Stack X's if multiple items have the same value
Add a title and label the number line
To analyze: count X's, find the most/least common values

examples.title: Pencil Lengths Line Plot
examples.text: Class measured pencil lengths: 4,5,5,5,6,6,7 inches. On the line plot, 5 has 3 X's (most common), 6 has 2 X's, and 4 and 7 each have 1 X.

examples.title: Analyzing a Line Plot
examples.text: On a line plot of books read: 0(2 X's), 1(5 X's), 2(4 X's), 3(3 X's). Most students read 1 book. The range is 0 to 3 books.

quiz.q: On a line plot, if the number 5 has 4 X's above it, what does that mean?
options: Four items have a value of 5
quiz.explanation: Each X represents one data point, so 4 X's above 5 means four items have a value of 5.

quiz.q: Which value is the most common on a line plot?
options: The number with the most X's
quiz.explanation: The number with the tallest stack of X's is the most common (the mode).
